source.title: Transcriptomic Profiling of the Biceps Femoris Long Head 72 h Following a Football Match and Associations With Recovery Biomarkers

paper.citation: Cosio P.L., Pinal‐Fernandez I., Moreno‐Simonet L., Cadefau J.A., Mammen A.L., Rodas G., et al. Transcriptomic Profiling of the Biceps Femoris Long Head 72 h Following a Football Match and Associations With Recovery Biomarkers. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2026;36(7):e70339. doi:10.1111/sms.70339.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What gene-expression and pathway-level changes remain in the biceps femoris long head three days after a high-load soccer match, and how are those changes associated with creatine kinase, hamstring rate of torque development, and sprint performance? Ten male outfield players from a regional first-division soccer competition participated; mean age was 20.6 years. One biopsy yielded insufficient RNA, leaving nine players for transcriptomic analyses. This was a secondary integrative analysis of a previously studied cohort with no non-match control group. Dominant-leg biceps femoris long-head biopsies were collected seven days before and 72 hours after a standardized FIFA-rules match.
paper.tldr: MYH1, which encodes type IIx myosin, was the only listed top gene that remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction, with downregulation at 72 hours. Pathway analysis showed coordinated positive enrichment in stress response, immune and cytokine signaling, protein turnover, mitochondrial quality control, translation, and structural remodeling, while muscle-contraction pathways were negatively enriched. Use the study as evidence that a fixed 72-hour calendar rule may miss ongoing hamstring recovery in some athletes, especially after high-speed exposure.
paper.methods: This was a secondary integrative analysis of a previously studied cohort with no non-match control group. Dominant-leg biceps femoris long-head biopsies were collected seven days before and 72 hours after a standardized FIFA-rules match. All players exceeded predefined match-load thresholds, then completed only low-volume recovery assessments for three days. Bulk RNA sequencing used paired linear modeling and false-discovery-rate correction; clinical measures included creatine kinase, hamstring rate of torque development to 100 milliseconds, and 40-m sprint performance before and at 24, 48, and 72 hours after the match.
paper.findings: MYH1, which encodes type IIx myosin, was the only listed top gene that remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction, with downregulation at 72 hours. Pathway analysis showed coordinated positive enrichment in stress response, immune and cytokine signaling, protein turnover, mitochondrial quality control, translation, and structural remodeling, while muscle-contraction pathways were negatively enriched. Creatine kinase remained elevated, early hamstring rate of torque development remained reduced, and sprint time remained slower than pre-match at 24, 48, and 72 hours in the nine-player subgroup. Transcriptomic pathways related to stress, apoptosis, immune response, protein metabolism, and remodeling were associated with changes in creatine kinase and rate of torque development. Reduced MYH1 expression was associated with larger decrements in hamstring rate of torque development, but these small-sample correlations are associative and exploratory. The combined molecular and clinical pattern indicates ongoing remodeling at 72 hours in this cohort; it does not define when every player is fully recovered.
paper.limitations: The final sample comprised only nine young male regional-level soccer players, with no control group and only two biopsy time points. The pre-match biopsy followed three days of rest, which may still have contained residual effects from earlier soccer exposure. Biopsy location, tissue heterogeneity, RNA processing, and sampling different sites can add technical and biological variation. Only one gene survived gene-level multiple-comparison correction, making pathway-level interpretations more prominent but not equivalent to direct protein or functional recovery. The standardized soccer match involved more than 10 km of running and substantial high-speed exposure, so direct transfer to collegiate American football is limited by sport, position, collision load, substitution patterns, and training schedule. Molecular remodeling also does not itself establish injury risk or contraindicate training.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the study as evidence that a fixed 72-hour calendar rule may miss ongoing hamstring recovery in some athletes, especially after high-speed exposure. For collegiate American football, integrate individual exposure, symptoms, prior injury, sprint readiness, force or rate-of-force-development measures, and schedule demands. Do not biopsy athletes or use creatine kinase alone to clear or restrict participation. A pragmatic application is to preserve individualized recovery options and avoid assuming that normal-looking wellness or time elapsed means complete tissue recovery.
